knowledge_point.title: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Product Rules

question.:question/worked-solution:
This question requires the product rule. Let $u(x)=x+1$ and $v(x)={e}^{14x}.$ Then

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=1,\,{v}^{′}(x)=14{e}^{14x}.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x) \\  & =(1)({e}^{14x})+(x+1)(14{e}^{14x}) \\  & ={e}^{14x}+14(x+1){e}^{14x} \\  & =(1+14(x+1)){e}^{14x} \\  & =(14x+15){e}^{14x}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
This question requires the product rule. Let $u(x)={e}^{11x}$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{ln}x.$ Then

$$
{u}^{'}(x)=11{e}^{11x},\,{v}^{'}(x)=\frac{1}{x}.

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={u}^{'}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{'}(x) \\  & =(11{e}^{11x})(\operatorname{ln}x)+({e}^{11x})\,(\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =(11\operatorname{ln}x+\frac{1}{x}){e}^{11x}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Product Rules

question.:question/worked-solution:
This question requires the product rule. Let $u(x)=x^{3}$ and $v(x)=(9 x^{2} + 1)^{3}.$ Then

$$
u^{′}(x)=3x^{2},\,v^{′}(x)=54x(9 x^{2} + 1)^{2}.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =u^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot v^{′}(x) \\  & =(3x^{2})((9 x^{2} + 1)^{3})+(x^{3})(54x(9 x^{2} + 1)^{2}) \\  & =3x^{2}(9 x^{2} + 1)^{3}+54x^{4}(9 x^{2} + 1)^{2} \\  & =(3x^{2}(9 x^{2} + 1)+54x^{4})(9 x^{2} + 1)^{2} \\  & =(81x^{4}+3x^{2})(9 x^{2} + 1)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
